newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian Serb president moves against rival police.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Serb president moves against rival police.

text.p: Police loyal to Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic moved to seize control of a building early on Sunday where they said rival police were tapping telephones used by the president, NATO officers and Serb media reported.

Hardline nationalists opposed to Plavsic asked permission from the NATO-led peace force to deploy their special police to counter the action but NATO rejected the request, alliance officers told Reuters.
The NATO-led Stabilisation Force (SFOR) later deployed peacekeeping troops to the station in the northwest town of Banja Luka to prevent possible violence, a SFOR spokesman said.
Colonel Steven Rausch said Plavsic's police had committed an "apparent violation" of new guidelines handed down by NATO, which has assumed supervision of all special police in Bosnia.
The incident was under investigation and he said Plavsic's police were being questioned at the public security centre in Banja Luka.
"Our primary interest is to see that this gets resolved in a non-violent way," Rausch said.

The police action reflected rising tensions in Bosnia's Serb territory where Plavsic supporters are waging a battle for power against loyalists of ex-president and indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic.
Western officials say Plavsic has been aware for some time that her office was under close surveillance from her rivals.

Dragan Lukac, a senior special police officer allied with Plavsic, said evidence was found that showed secret police loyal to Karadzic had "continuously tapped" the president's telephone conversations and monitored faxes in and out of her office, the Belgrade-based Beta news agency reported.
Plavsic's police entered the station without any violence at about 4:30 a.m. (0230 GMT), Rausch said.
At about 11 a.m. (0900 GMT), Momcilo Krajisnik, an ally of Karadzic and the Serb member of Bosnia's collective presidency, rang SFOR asking to meet about an "urgent" matter.
"Krajisnik said he wanted to deploy RS (Serb republic) specialist police for an operational matter," Rausch said. "That permission was denied by SFOR," he added.
In addition to Plavsic, state security tapped the phones of constitutional court judges Rajko Kuzmanovic and Jovo Rosic, Lukac told a Banja Luka radio station.
Rosic was badly beaten last Thursday because he opposed plans for the court to strike down a decision by Plavsic to dissolve parliament and call early elections, independent Serb media reported.
Rosic was concussed and spent the weekend in hospital in Banja Luka, where soldiers loyal to Plavsic guarded his room, Serb media said.

With Rosic absent from the seven-member court, the remaining judges declared Plavsic's move unconstitutional last Friday but gave no explanation for the ruling. Karadzic's allies had pushed through the court decision in a bid to gain the upper hand in their power struggle with Plavsic.

"This is a sign that the SDS (ruling party) has no more political arguments left and must start applying physical repression," Miodrag Zivanovic, leader of the opposition Social Liberal Party, said. REUTER
